http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/13/us-st.text: US airstrikes against Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen last year resulted in the deaths of over 150 civilians, according to a Pentagon assessment released on Wednesday.The Pentagon review, which was sent to Congress as part of an annual report on civilian casualties, focused on three airstrikes in April 2025 conducted in response to the Houthi attacks on commercial ships in the Red Sea, a crucial global trade route that connects the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean.The US strikes targeted hostile forces in or near Houthi-controlled capital Sana'a as well as the Ras Isa port. A total of 153 civilians were killed, and 243 were injured, according to the report.The strike on the port was the most deadly, killing 80 people and injuring 171 others. At the time, the Houthis published graphic footage of the aftermath on their al-Masirah satellite news channel, showing casualties in the port.The US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, said at the time that the “strike was not intended to harm the people of Yemen.”“US forces took action to eliminate this source of fuel for the Iran-backed Houthi terrorists and deprive them of illegal revenue that has funded Houthi efforts to terrorise the entire region for over 10 years,” CENTCOM said in its statement.The command determined that the three strikes “more likely than not” resulted in civilian harm, the review said. The information was based on US intelligence sources, imagery and open-source reporting.Concerns have continued to grow among US lawmakers and human rights groups over civilian casualties in military operations during US President Donald Trump's second term, after a US missile struck a primary school in Minab in the opening days of the Iran war, killing up to 168 people.Condolence payments to victimsThe Pentagon review also considered whether condolence payments should be made to victims or their families, but determined that they were not appropriate in the three cases. The review did not explain why.The payments are one option available to the US military when civilians are killed or injured during military operations. They are not required by law and do not constitute an admission of wrongdoing.The US has made similar payments in previous cases. After a US drone strike in Afghanistan in 2021 mistakenly killed 10 civilians, including seven children, the Pentagon said it was committed to offering condolence payments to the victims' relatives.The Houthis, which are part of Iran's loose network of proxies Tehran calls "Axis of Resistance," said the attacks on ships in the Red Sea that led to the US strikes were in support of Palestinians amid the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza.The group has since threatened to close the Bab el-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea to global shipping, while reports emerged that it is also mulling introducing a transit fee following consultations with Tehran.The Strait of Hormuz — another crucial global shipping chokepoint — has been nearly completely shut to cargo vessel traffic since the beginning of the Iran war in late February.A simultaneous closure of both straits would affect roughly one third of global oil trade.

Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham took over from Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, shortly after parliament’s summer recess began. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA Andy Burnham More public control is the way to grow UK economy, Burnham to tell MPs Exclusive: Prime minister wants to ‘bring back hope’ by tackling cost of living as MPs call for electoral reform Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor Mon 31 Aug 2026 14.13 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 17.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham will drive home his pledge to bring more essential services back into public control, telling MPs in the Commons on Tuesday that it will be the only way to improve growth across the country. Burnham will address the house for the first time in 16 years from the frontbench, and six weeks since he became prime minister, after spending the summer recess announcing a slew of policies that will now be put before MPs. He will use the statement to put public control of services at the heart of his priorities for the coming months, sources told the Guardian, saying he would make the case that it would unlock investment, jobs and growth. Burnham will say that the cost of everyday services to family budgets is holding back the economy and promise a plan to regain control of the costs. A No 10 source said: “Andy is optimistic about our country’s future. He has a clear plan for how we turn things round. He is determined we make this the moment we bring back hope.” The prime minister will face an early test of his commitment to public control as he mulls legislation to make it easier to bring struggling utilities such as Thames Water under government ownership. The Guardian reported last week Burnham was considering laws to make it easier to put companies into insolvency proceedings and then take control of them afterwards. View image in fullscreen The prime minister has said taking water companies such as Thames Water into public control is crucial to his vision for the country. Photograph: Maureen McLean/Shutterstock He will also face crunch decisions on possible changes to the immigration bill to exempt carers, as well as pressure from MPs to back moves towards electoral reform. A quasi-judicial decision on whether to allow more North Sea drilling is also expected soon: a highly divisive issue within the party . Burnham will tell MPs that he wants to “bring back hope” in politics and pledge to work constructively with opposition parties. On Monday, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, sacked her shadow chancellor Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Priti Patel, promoting Andrew Griffith in Stride’s place in the hope of making further inroads in attacking Burnham’s economic approach. Patel is replaced by Tom Tugendhat . View image in fullscreen Andrew Griffith, right, with Kemi Badenoch and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, second from right, during a visit to Godalming, Surrey earlier this year. Photograph: Ben Whitley/PA Burnham will give a scathing analysis of how privatised services have done little for the public, saying that utilities and transport have not been run in the public interest and are neither reliable nor affordable. He will point to action already being taken to bring more bus routes under public control, including through a partnership between No 10 North and the West Midlands Combined Authority. The Liverpool City Region will start taking control of bus services from next weekend. Burnham has promised a 10-year project to take public control of utilities which is expected to be a major focus of his next few months in power. Allies have said the prime minister is “completely committed” to putting utilities such as energy and water companies into public control, and is looking at every option. As well as setting out key priorities for his first months in office, Burnham will face a two-hour grilling from MPs about policies announced over the summer – including a cut to VAT on energy bills, £2 bus fares, the scrapping of digital ID, a major expansion of devolution and a plan for a national care service. Opposition MPs are expected to ask tough questions on how the pledges will be funded as well as how Burnham expects to fill a £4.7bn gap in the defence investment plan left by his predecessor, Keir Starmer. On Tuesday, the justice secretary, Alex Norris, will also present the government’s plans to cut the number of prisoners eligible for early release, including the killers of PC Andrew Harper. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Though the decision will see most of those convicted of manslaughter remain in prison to serve longer sentences, it has also raised alarm that the number of prison places may reach crisis point faster. Why are prisons overcrowded? Because no government will stand up to the tabloids | Zoe Williams Read more Later in the week, Burnham will face Badenoch for his first prime minister’s questions and will also need to navigate the growing number of Labour MPs who are heaping pressure on him to toughen up the representation of the people bill which returns to the Commons this week. Nearly 100 MPs have called on Burnham to back a commission on electoral reform , given the prime minister has previously been a vociferous supporter of changing the voting system. MPs have also been angered by the decision to drop any cap on party donations, after pressure from trade unions, despite the prime minister having previously backed a cap of £500,000 . The Liberal Democrats said on Monday they would put their full backing behind an amendment from the Labour MP Alex Sobel that calls for a commission on electoral reform to be established within 100 days. The party’s leader, Ed Davey , said it was a chance for Burnham to prove he was different to Starmer. “Reform stand to benefit from our terrible voting system and could manipulate it all the way to No 10,” he said. Davey added: “Keir Starmer never would have agreed to a national commission. He failed to grasp that it is our role as progressives to fix the broken system the Conservatives created. The only question now is: what kind of politician is Andy Burnham? Is he willing to do the right thing?” Reform will host its party conference this week in Birmingham, with Farage speaking on Friday. In the latest poll from More in Common, Labour hold a four-point lead over Reform, with the Tories a point behind. The latest Opinium poll found that Burnham’s net approval rating had increased over the last fortnight by three points. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27933.text: Big News Network.com Slovak PM Fico ready for snap election in January BRATISLAVA, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said Sunday that he was ready for a snap parliamentary election as early as January if the governing coalition can no longer secure a majority in Parliament, according to the News Agency of the Slovak Republic (TASR). Fico said an early election could be held by adopting a constitutional law to shorten the current parliamentary term. "It's not in my hands. I'm here to govern this country, but you can only do that if you have your back covered by Parliament," Fico said. He added that if an early election becomes necessary, it should be held as soon as possible rather than being postponed until June. The prime minister said he was prepared to accept an election in January, while Slovak National Party (SNS) leader Andrej Danko and Environment Minister Tomas Taraba, an SNS nominee, would have to decide whether they wanted the government to continue until the next regular election scheduled for 2027. "If Danko and Taraba want to leave, then I ask them to put an end to this circus. Let them provide guarantees and the government will carry on. If they don't provide guarantees and bring down the government, there will be a snap general election," Fico said. The remarks came amid a dispute between Danko and Taraba, which has raised questions over whether the governing coalition can maintain its parliamentary majority. Taraba has indicated that he could return to Parliament as an independent lawmaker if he leaves the government. His move could further weaken Fico's coalition, which has only a narrow majority in the 150-seat Parliament, potentially making it harder for the government to pass legislation. Fico said he did not want to participate in the dispute between Danko and Taraba. Meanwhile, Fico said his Smer-SD party was prepared to move into opposition following the next parliamentary election if necessary.
